title: Sesshin, the last day
hook: stillness, and the tea at the end

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first days of sesshin: the wall, the bells, the stick asked for with a bow. Your line was sore legs. What did your body complain about, and what did you notice? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

By the last morning of sesshin, the hall sounds different. The same bells, the same wall, the same rows of cushions. But the shuffling has stopped. Nobody is shifting their weight every few minutes. The ache in the knee may still be there, but the arguing about it has gone quiet. Then the final bell rings, and it doesn't call anyone to sit again. Someone comes down the row with a kettle. A small cup is set in front of each person, and tea is poured. Today: sesshin, the last day.
screen: `THE SHUFFLING STOPS.` → `THE FINAL BELL.` → `A KETTLE COMES DOWN THE ROW.`

segments.voice: First, the stillness. Some students who sit sesshin describe the later days as quieter, not because the mind has gone blank, but because it has stopped fighting the schedule. The bells ring and the body goes. Sitting has become ordinary. Some Zen teachers say that ordinariness is closer to the point than any fireworks. Second, tea in Zen. Tea and Zen have kept company for a long time in China and Japan. Tradition says monks drank it to stay awake through long sittings, and serving tea became a practice in its own right, done with full attention. Some sesshins end with tea served in the hall, simply, in silence, before talking begins. Third, an old Zen story. The Chinese teacher Zhaozhou asks a newly arrived monk, have you been here before? Yes, says the monk. Zhaozhou says, go have some tea. He asks another, have you been here before? No, says the second monk. Go have some tea. The temple steward, puzzled, asks: why tell both of them the same thing? Zhaozhou calls his name. The steward answers. Zhaozhou says, go have some tea. Whatever you've done or not done, whatever you know or don't, the next thing is the cup in front of you. Fourth, the tea at the end. After days of effort, the last teaching is a warm cup held in two hands, drunk slowly, with nothing to achieve. The sesshin doesn't end with an insight announced. It ends with tea, and then people get up, wash the cups, and go home.
screen: `STILLNESS IS ORDINARY.` · `TEA, DRUNK WITH FULL ATTENTION.` · `ZHAOZHOU: GO HAVE SOME TEA.` · `NOTHING LEFT TO ACHIEVE.` · then, large: `THE TEA AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's a way to try it, if you'd like. If you have a cup of tea, or coffee, or just water, hold it now in both hands. If not, hold your empty hands as if there were a cup in them. Feel the warmth or the coolness. Notice its weight. Bring it to your lips slowly, and take one small sip, tasting it fully. Set it down. Breathe. Then another sip. Nothing to figure out, nothing to finish. Just this cup, and then this one. The bell holds the time.
Sesshin. A Zen retreat of several days, which, in some halls, ends not with a speech but with stillness, and a small cup of tea. Today's word.
Your line: the tea at the end. Today, drink one cup of something slowly, with both hands, and do nothing else while you drink it. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Zen sesshin end in different ways from hall to hall; in some, tea is served to each sitter in silence before the retreat closes and talking resumes, and tea itself is prepared and drunk as a practice of attention in Zen communities.

fork.setup: you're the temple steward. Zhaozhou just told two newcomers, one who'd been there and one who hadn't, to go have some tea. you ask him why. what does he do?
options: calls your name, and tells you to go have some tea.
fork.reveal: he calls the steward's name, the steward answers, and Zhaozhou says: go have some tea. the answer is the cup in front of you.

original.note: Sanskrit dhyana, meditative absorption; the name Chan in Chinese and Zen in Japanese is traced to it.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of a Zen retreat is a big moment of insight.
what it means: the last day is stillness made ordinary, and a cup of tea drunk slowly with nothing to achieve.
what a scholar hears: Zhaozhou's 'go have some tea', given to the one who came before, the one who didn't, and the one who asked why.

sources.ref: Recorded sayings of Zhaozhou (Zhaozhou Congshen), 'go have some tea'

notes: Zhaozhou's 'go have some tea' (chi cha qu) story paraphrased: two newcomers asked whether they had been there before, both told to have tea; the temple head (yuanzhu) asks why; Zhaozhou calls his name and tells him to have tea. Confirm details and source (recorded sayings / later lamp records).
Tea in Zen: monks drinking tea to stay awake through sitting, and tea preparation as practice. General; confirm.
'Some sesshins end with tea served in the hall' is hedged; practice differs. Confirm.
'Students who sit sesshin describe the later days as quieter' is general retreat lore; confirm or soften.
Original: dhyana (ध्यान), with Chan/Zen traced to it; standard but confirm the phrasing satisfies the claims rule.

Editor: in the story the questioner is the temple steward (yuanzhu), not the head of the monastery (Zhaozhou was the abbot); fixed in teach, match and fork. Tea-to-stay-awake now 'tradition says'; 'students describe' softened to 'some students'; the narrator's claim about what Zen points at is now attributed to some teachers.
